title: Breast cancer prevention and treatment misinformation on Twitter: An analysis of two languages
screen_reason: Content analysis of 6,221 breast-cancer tweets (Jan 2018 - Mar 2022) in English and Malay; the 780 tweets about prevention or treatment were coded for accuracy by an oncologist and a pharmacist against clinical guidelines and peer-reviewed evidence. 456 (58.5%) contained misinformation, with language-specific shares (Malay 358/428 = 83.6%; English 98/352 = 27.8%). These are CONTENT prevalence estimates with explicit denominators.

estimates.country: not stated - tweets were selected by language (English or Malay), with no geographic restriction; the study is framed on the Malaysian context
estimates.measure_type: % of breast-cancer prevention/treatment tweets that contain misinformation (English and Malay pooled)
estimates.value_raw: From the 780 tweets analysed for content accuracy, 456 (58.5%) misinformation was identified
estimates.denominator: 780 tweets about breast cancer prevention or treatment (352 English, 428 Malay), drawn from 6,221 collected tweets by 4,245 unique users
estimates.definition: A tweet was coded as misinformation if it was 'inaccurate' (inaccurate, misleading or exaggerated benefits or dangers compared to actual scientific evidence) or 'fabricated' (no evidence of the claim in the scientific literature); linked external sources were also checked for accuracy
estimates.misinfo_def: 'we use the term "misinformation" as an umbrella term to describe health-related false information, giving the benefit of the doubt to the users involved, as the intent is not always clear'
estimates.source_quote: Results: There were 780 tweets related to breast cancer prevention and treatment, and 456 (58.5%) contain misinformation, with signiﬁcantly more misinformation in Malay compared to English tweets (OR = 6.18, 95% CI: 3.45–11.07, p < 0.001).
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Categorisation and sources of misinformation', p. 4; also Abstract ('There were 780 tweets related to breast cancer prevention and treatment, and 456 (58.5%) contain misinformation')
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two coders - a pharmacist (IY) and an oncologist (NFAM) - independently rated accuracy, type and content; discrepancies resolved by a third person (a pharmacy lecturer, NMS). Accuracy judged on clinical knowledge or cross-referenced with breast cancer clinical practice guidelines and peer-reviewed journal articles. Cohen's kappa 0.874 (English) and 0.887 (Malay)
estimates.moderator_quote: We aimed for at least 3000 tweets for each language, using the keywords 'breast cancer' for English tweets and 'kanser payudara' or 'kanser payu dara' for Malay tweets... all Malay tweets from the data collection period were included for screening, and tweets in English were randomly selected from different periods based on computer-generated random sequences using Python.
estimates.notes: IMPORTANT CAVEAT: this pooled 58.5% is an artefact of the sampling design, not a population estimate. The two language corpora were sampled on completely different bases - ALL 3,167 available Malay tweets, versus 3,054 English tweets randomly drawn from 344,736 - so the 55%/45% Malay/English mix of the 780-tweet denominator is arbitrary. The two language rows below are the interpretable estimates; use EITHER this pooled row OR the two language rows, never both.

estimates.notes: COUNTRY JUDGEMENT CALL: the corpus is defined by language, never geolocated, so I coded Global; an adjudicator who treats Malay-language Twitter as effectively Malaysian would code country_norm=Malaysia. Note the very high share is partly driven by product sellers: 175 of the 199 seller tweets were Malay, and 189/199 (95.0%) of seller tweets carried misinformation. Language split of the pooled row - do not aggregate with it.

estimates.definition: Coded as misinformation if 'inaccurate' (inaccurate, misleading or exaggerated benefits/dangers versus actual scientific evidence) or 'fabricated' (no evidence of the claim in the scientific literature)

estimates.notes: The English corpus is a random subsample of a very large keyword pool, so this 27.8% is the closer analogue of a random-sample content estimate. Language split of the pooled row - do not aggregate with it. The Malay/English contrast is the paper's headline (OR = 6.18, 95% CI 3.45-11.07).

estimates.country: not stated - tweets selected by language (English or Malay), no geographic restriction
estimates.measure_type: % of breast-cancer prevention/treatment tweets containing FABRICATED misinformation (stricter definition: claims with no evidence in the scientific literature)
estimates.value_raw: 233 fabricated of the 456 misinformation tweets ('Among these, 233 (51.1%) contained fabricated information'), out of the 780 prevention/treatment tweets analysed: 233/780 = 29.9%
estimates.denominator: 780 tweets about breast cancer prevention or treatment (the same denominator as the pooled row)
estimates.definition: Tweets coded 'Fabricated' - 'Tweets with no evidence of the claim in the scientific literature' (Table 1), the stricter of the two misinformation types (the other being 'Inaccurate')
estimates.misinfo_def: 'we use the term "misinformation" as an umbrella term to describe health-related false information, giving the benefit of the doubt to the users involved, as the intent is not always clear'
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Content of misinformation', p. 5; type definitions in Table 1
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Pharmacist and oncologist coded independently, third-person adjudication; kappa 0.874 (English) / 0.887 (Malay)
estimates.moderator_quote: Fabricated: Tweets with no evidence of the claim in the scientific literature. Example: 'Cure breast cancer through yoga meditation. No diet. No medicine.' (Table 1)
estimates.notes: STRICTER-BREADTH VARIANT of the pooled row: 233 and 780 are both verbatim counts over the same denominator, so 233/780 is an exact part/whole share permitted by R8 (it is NOT a cross-category sum or a complement). It is offered so the review can see how much of the 58.5% survives a fabricated-only definition. within_misinfo_content is false because the denominator is the full 780-tweet sample, not the misinformation subset; the paper's own 51.1% (233/456) IS a within-misinfo figure and was not used as the value. Inherits the same sampling-mixture caveat as the pooled row.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) Within-misinformation type splits by language were not extracted (they are within_misinfo_content figures and would multiply rows): English 68/98 (69.4%) fabricated and 30 (30.6%) inaccurate; Malay 165/358 (46.1%) fabricated and 193 (53.9%) inaccurate. The overall 'inaccurate' counterpart of my fabricated row (223/780 = 28.6%) was left out to avoid two rows partitioning the same estimate. (2) Table 3's other cross-tabs are determinant subgroups, not headline splits, and were not made into rows: product sellers 189/199 (95.0%) vs non-sellers 267/581 (46.0%); before COVID-19 319/455 (70.1%) vs after 137/325 (42.2%); non-BCAM months 398/637 (62.5%) vs October 58/143 (40.6%); no external source 231/268 (86.2%), miscellaneous sources 215/258 (83.3%), official/peer-reviewed sources 10/254 (3.9%). The source-of-information split is striking (3.9% vs 86.2%) and an adjudicator may want it. (3) Screening-stage shares are not misinformation prevalence: 3,261/6,221 (52.4%) not medically related; 1,646 (61.2%) of medically related tweets on epidemiology/screening/risk/symptoms; 780 (29.0%) on prevention and treatment. (4) Content-theme shares are computed within the misinformation set (food & lifestyle 175/240 (72.9%) inaccurate; alternative therapy 134/158 (84.8%) fabricated; supplements 20/38 (52.6%) fabricated; sellers 153/196 (78.1%) of supplement/alternative misinformation) - within-misinfo detail, not prevalence. (5) 'Posts containing misinformation ranged from 30 to 51%' in the Introduction is cited from other studies (R8) and was not extracted. (6) Regression odds ratios (Malay OR = 6.18; sellers OR = 4.03) are associations.

rob.design: Quali-quantitative cross-sectional content analysis of Twitter. Public Twitter API, tweets posted Jan 2018 - Mar 2022, keywords 'breast cancer' (English) and 'kanser payudara'/'kanser payu dara' (Malay). ALL 3,167 available Malay tweets were screened; 3,054 English tweets were randomly selected (Python-generated random sequences) from 344,736, with October (Breast Cancer Awareness Month) tweets purposively collected each year. After de-duplication and relevance screening, 6,221 tweets from 4,245 unique users; 780 concerned prevention or treatment and were assessed for accuracy. Coding: pharmacist (IY) and oncologist (NFAM) independently, third-person adjudication (NMS), judged against clinical practice guidelines and peer-reviewed literature, with linked external sources also verified; Cohen's kappa 0.874 (English) and 0.887 (Malay). Ethics approval JEP-2022-240. Stated limitations: Malay data relatively scarce (Twitter is not Malaysians' most used platform); Twitter skews young while breast cancer is commoner in older people; single platform. The unequal sampling of the two language corpora means the pooled figure should not be read as a population prevalence.
rob.item6_quote: Inaccurate: Tweets containing inaccurate, misleading, or exaggerated benefits or dangers compared to actual scientific evidence. Fabricated: Tweets with no evidence of the claim in the scientific literature. (Table 1)
rob.item10_quote: From the 780 tweets analysed for content accuracy, 456 (58.5%) misinformation was identified.
